  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
# Rosa's Story

Rosa María Delgado had spent fifty-two years in the profession she loved. At seventy-four, she had mentored three generations of pharmacy technicians, earned the trust of her community, and built a reputation for meticulous attention to detail and unshakeable composure under pressure. These qualities had defined her—the pharmacist who never made a mistake, who could manage a busy counter with grace, who patients asked for by name. She had believed, until the winter of two years ago, that these were permanent features of who she was.

Her marriage to Héctor had lasted forty-six years. The final six months had been different—he drank more, his words grew sharper, his hands grew harder. On a Tuesday evening in January, after she had questioned a charge on the credit card, he had shoved her against the kitchen counter, then onto the floor. His fists had come down on her ribs, her shoulders, her back. She had curled inward, her body folding to protect itself, and she had remained in that position for what felt like hours though it was only minutes. When it ended, she lay on the tile floor with her face turned to the side, unable to move, unable to cry out. The shame had come first, before the pain—the thought that this was somehow her fault, that she had provoked it, that she had become the kind of woman this happened to.

She had told no one. Not her daughter in Phoenix, not her sister in San Juan, not even her doctor when she came in with bruised ribs two weeks later. But something had fractured. Her body no longer felt like her own. When she showered, she avoided looking down at the still-discolored skin on her torso. She had come to believe that to see her own body was to see evidence of her weakness, and so she dressed quickly, kept her eyes forward, and tried not to inhabit the physical form that had betrayed her by being vulnerable.

The pharmacy became harder. She found herself listening to the ambient sounds of the store—the beep of the register, the shuffle of feet—with a new kind of attention. Whenever someone approached the counter with any force, or when a customer opened the heavy pharmacy door with a bang, her entire body would stiffen. Her heart would race. She would grip the counter. A colleague had asked her if she was well; she had said only that the lighting was bothering her eyes. The truth was that she was monitoring, always, for the sound of someone entering. At home, she had begun leaving lights on in every room, even though Héctor had moved out in February—she had finally told him to leave, though she had told everyone else he was visiting family. She kept the door to her bedroom locked. She slept poorly, her body tense even in sleep, as though braced for impact.

The comments from her family had become unbearable. Her daughter had called in March asking when she would be ready to have people over for Easter; her sister had sent a message saying it was time to move forward. These remarks, meant as gentle encouragement, had triggered a panic in her that was difficult to name. To allow herself to feel close to anyone, to let someone into her home, to be vulnerable in the presence of another person—these things now felt dangerous in a way she could not articulate. She had declined the invitations. She had kept conversations brief. She had, without quite realizing it, begun to withdraw.

By summer, she had taken a leave from the pharmacy. She had told her supervisor she needed time for her health, which was true in a way she could not fully explain. What she could not say was that she no longer trusted herself to be the person she had always been—that the pharmacist who never made mistakes felt gone, replaced by someone fragile and unreliable. When she looked back on who she had been, it seemed like a different person entirely, someone she no longer had access to.

It was her daughter, visiting unexpectedly in September, who had finally insisted. Rosa had flinched when her daughter had tried to embrace her. She had not answered the door immediately when her daughter had knocked, afraid of the sound. Her daughter had seen the locked bedroom door, the untouched kitchen, the woman her mother had become. "Mamá," she had said, "something happened. And you need to tell someone who can help."

Rosa sits now in the waiting room, her purse held tightly in her lap, afraid of what it might mean to speak the truth aloud, but more afraid of continuing to live as she has been—isolated, ashamed, and convinced that the strength she once possessed is gone forever.
